title: Stocks Up Pre-Bell as Traders Parse President Trump's Latest Comments on Iran War
detail:
PREMIUM
Stocks Up Pre-Bell as Traders Parse President Trump's Latest Comments on Iran War
MT Newswires

^GSPC
^DJI
^NDX
stock trading market equity wall street -Shutterstock

The benchmark US stock measures were pointing higher before the open Friday as traders assess President Donald Trump's latest comments on the war with Iran.

The S&P 500 edged up 0.1%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3% in premarket activity, while the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.1%. Equity markets finished the previous trading session in the green.

In an interview with Newsmax on Thursday, Trump said he isn't considering sending ground troops into Iran.

Trump's comments came after CNN reported, citing sources, that the US military has developed plans that include the potential use of a so-called "mother of all bombs" to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.

"The mother of all bombs is not nuclear," Trump said in the Newsmax interview. "This is just an extremely large bomb."

Trump said the US may have to strike Iran's Pickaxe mountain, a suspected nuclear site, but he doesn't see ground troops being deployed for such an operation, Newsmax reported. The US leader also said Iran is negotiating with Washington and expressed confidence that the war in the Middle East "will be over very soon."

West Texas Intermediate crude oil decreased 0.6% to $97.39 a barrel early Friday, while Brent dipped 0.2% to $105.73.

The International Energy Agency on Thursday outlined plans to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel "as soon as possible" as part of its efforts to address a global supply crunch. In March, the agency agreed to release a record 400 million barrels of oil in a bid to stem crude prices and address supply disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict.

Treasury yields were mixed, with the two-year rate retreating 0.5 basis points to 4.75% while the 10-year rate gained 1.3 basis points to 5.1%.

Government data showed Thursday producer prices jumped at the fastest pace in more than four years in September amid a surge in energy costs, a day after a report showed consumer inflation also accelerated last month.

Retail sales growth exceeded expectations in September as outlays at gas stations increased amid elevated fuel prices, the Census Bureau reported Thursday.

"With core inflation running at 2.6% year-on-year and oil prices remaining elevated, which increases the risk that price pressures spread to other categories, the (Federal Reserve) likely will not be able to remain on the sidelines for much longer," TD Economics Economist Admir Kolaj said in a Thursday note.

Despite the hot inflation reports, markets are currently pricing in an 85% probability that the Fed will keep its benchmark rate steady later this month, up from 72% on Thursday, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The remaining odds are in favor of a 25-basis-point hike.

Friday's economic calendar has the import and export prices report for September, followed by the industrial production report for the same month and the weekly Baker Hughes oil-and-gas rig count.

Travelers (TRV), Truist Financial (TFC), M&T Bank (MTB), Citizens Financial (CFG) and Regions Financial (RF) report their latest financial results before the bell.

Shares of Tesla (TSLA) jumped 4.3% pre-bell after the electric vehicle manufacturer unveiled its new Roadster car capable of flight using cold-gas thrusters. Nike (NKE) added 0.9% after closing the previous session with an increase of 5.2%.

J.B. Hunt Transport Services (JBHT) was down 1.3% as its third-quarter operating income as a percentage of revenue declined year over year.

Spot gold inclined 0.8% to $4,203 per troy ounce, while bitcoin traded down 0.3% at $82,080.

Tesla shares rose nearly 5% in premarket trading after the electric vehicle maker unveiled its new Roadster model during a live demonstration on Thursday evening. The event at SpaceX's McGregor, Texas, test facility showcased the vehicle using pressurized air to perform a controlled jump and correct its orientation before landing on all four wheels.

Chief Executive Elon Musk said production of the long-awaited vehicle was set to begin in 2028, adding "actually" as he outlined the timeline. The demonstration renewed investor attention on the Roadster as Tesla continues to develop its broader vehicle and technology ambitions.

Strategy fell 3% in premarket trading after MSCI announced new rules that could result in the company being excluded from its indexes. The decision followed a consultation on the eligibility of non-operating companies and is scheduled to take effect with the November index review.

Under the new methodology, MSCI will assess companies using screens for operating assets and five financial ratios, replacing interim restrictions that had targeted firms with digital asset holdings accounting for at least 50% of total assets. The potential exclusion adds uncertainty for Strategy, whose substantial digital asset exposure has made it a focal point of debates over index eligibility.

Netflix dropped 2% in premarket trading after announcing a leadership change in its content division. Peter Rice, the former chairman of Walt Disney Television, will join the streaming company as chief content officer on October 26, replacing Bela Bajaria, who is leaving after nearly a decade at Netflix.

Strategists led by Michael Hartnett said the Fed needs to hike on Oct. 28 and flagged oil and the U.S., Iran, Russia, and Ukraine situations as key risks, as well as the rising chance of a "wave-like" Democratic sweep in the midterms.

On the AI front, the strategists said spenders and lenders are under pressure. Private equity and business development company ETFs are back at their 2026 lows, and Oracle's (NYSE:ORCL) credit default swaps are a stress point.

Hartnett and his team expect an October Fed hike "to restore credibility," noting CPI has been above the Fed's 2% target for 66 consecutive months. They said a hike should push long-end Treasury yields down another 20 basis points in coming weeks, limiting downside for risk assets.

That holds as long as AI financing fears ease and the U.S. and China avoid new spats after the midterms, the strategists said. Xi and Trump are due to meet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 and at the G20 in Miami on Dec. 14.

The team said it is adding exposure to "peak yield" beneficiaries, including small caps, REITs and especially consumer discretionary. Investors are the most underweight consumer discretionary since July 2008, per BofA's October fund manager survey.

Looking into 2027, the strategists said markets will be driven by AI and urge investors to keep an eye on semiconductor prices. Fresh gains would be bullish, while a rollover would signal tighter AI credit and a peak in AI capex growth, they added.

South Korea's KOSPI climbed 2.1%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 advanced 1.7%, recovering some of Thursday's steep losses as semiconductor stocks regained ground.

The MSCI Asia Pacific index rose 1.1%. The rebound followed Thursday's nearly 8% plunge in the KOSPI, which took the index to its lowest close since late July and triggered a circuit breaker amid heavy selling in memory-chip makers.

Indonesia's stocks bucked the regional recovery, with the Jakarta Composite down 10.8% at 5,233.00, after falling more than 11% earlier, in its steepest one-day decline since January 1998, after MSCI proposed reclassifying the country from emerging-market to standalone-market status.

In U.S. futures, Nasdaq 100 futures and S&P 500 futures were little changed, pointing to a more cautious start after Wall Street's cash indexes posted modest gains on Thursday.

Chipmakers rebound, but AI financing concerns persist

South Korean memory-chip makers led the recovery, with Samsung Electronics rising 2.6% and SK Hynix gaining 0.8%. Japan's Kioxia advanced 3.8%, while Sony rose 1.9%. Taiwan's Largan fell 3.1% and Foxconn rose 1.1%.

The rebound followed a technology selloff intensified by concerns about the financial risks underpinning the AI investment boom, particularly the debt burden of cloud-computing company CoreWeave.

Its shares recovered some ground on Thursday after extending Wednesday's 15.5% slump early in the session, when reports that its bond yields had reached distressed-debt levels helped fuel a broader global selloff in AI-linked stocks.

The selloff also reflected worries over Chinese competition after ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) reported progress on a next-generation DRAM architecture that could intensify competition with established manufacturers such as SK Hynix and Samsung. CXMT shares rebounded nearly 5% on Friday.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng gained 0.4%, China's CSI 300 rose 0.1% and the Shanghai Composite added 0.2%.
